events.title: The first concert
events.text: The Philharmonic Society of New York plays its first concert at the Apollo Rooms. Its seasons stay tiny for decades, four to six concerts a year, so early chart positions swing on a single night.

events.title: Carnegie Hall
events.text: The orchestra’s first subscription concert at Carnegie Hall, under Anton Seidl. Seidl was a Wagner specialist, and in his first five seasons Wagner’s share rose from 9% to 14%.

sources.text: Program 1678; Wagner share from the conductor analysis

events.title: “From the New World”
events.text: Seidl conducts the world premiere of Dvořák’s Ninth Symphony. In Seidl’s first five seasons Dvořák’s share of the subscription series doubled, from 4% to 9%.

events.title: Mahler on the podium
events.text: Gustav Mahler conducts the Philharmonic for the first time, then leads it for two seasons, conducting 85% of the subscription concerts himself. Wagner reaches a fifth of everything played. In January 1910 a pianist’s rehearsal-room fight with him makes the papers.

events.title: Concerts for young people
events.text: The first concert the archive files as a Young People’s Concert. The series is still running.

events.title: Living German composers disappear
events.text: After the US enters the First World War, the Metropolitan Opera suspends German opera (November 1917). At the Philharmonic, Richard Strauss, the most-played living German composer, is heard on January 3–4, 1918, then not again until December 9, 1920. Dead German composers mostly keep playing: Beethoven and Brahms barely move, though Wagner falls to 6% of the subscription series in 1918-19.

events.title: Summers at the Stadium
events.text: The first Lewisohn Stadium concert in the Philharmonic’s own records. Open-air summers add about 200 performances a year, leaning harder than the main season on Wagner, Tchaikovsky, Johann Strauss II and Gershwin. The last Stadium summer in the data is 1964.

events.title: A merger, and a premiere
events.text: In 1928 Walter Damrosch’s New York Symphony merges into the Philharmonic. That December, Damrosch conducts the world premiere of Gershwin’s An American in Paris.

sources.text: Merger: Wikipedia, New York Symphony Orchestra

events.title: On national radio
events.text: The first live national broadcast, over CBS, with Erich Kleiber conducting. The radio audience is now far larger than the hall.

events.title: The first classical LP
events.text: Columbia’s ML-4001, the first classical long-playing record, is the Philharmonic under Bruno Walter in Mendelssohn’s Violin Concerto with Nathan Milstein. The LP era is when Vivaldi, Baroque concertos and complete Mahler cycles come into reach.

sources.text: Wikipedia: Mendelssohn Violin Concerto (Nathan Milstein album)

events.title: Four shows a day at the Roxy
events.text: Dimitri Mitropoulos takes the orchestra into the Roxy movie palace, playing between film screenings, up to four times a day. This is the season that looked like a spike until same-day shows were collapsed.

events.title: Bernstein on television
events.text: CBS airs the first of Leonard Bernstein’s 53 televised Young People’s Concerts. Bernstein becomes music director that fall; his champions on the chart include Copland, Ives, William Schuman, Haydn and Mahler.

events.title: The Mahler centennial
events.text: A festival for Mahler’s 100th birthday runs to April 1960. Bernstein (25), Mitropoulos (16) and Bruno Walter (4) share the 45 performances, and Mahler is #2 for the season. Centenaries are the strongest anniversaries in the data.

events.title: Lincoln Center
events.text: Philharmonic Hall opens at Lincoln Center (renamed Avery Fisher Hall in 1973, and David Geffen Hall in 2015).

events.title: Concerts in the Parks
events.text: Free summer concerts in the city’s parks begin, the summer after the last Stadium season.

events.title: Boulez and the Rug Concerts
events.text: Pierre Boulez pulls the seats out of Philharmonic Hall and puts the audience on the floor for new music. His Prospective Encounters series follows in 1975, also built around new music.

events.title: Mozart’s bicentennial
events.text: For the 200th anniversary of Mozart’s death, Mozart is 22% of everything the orchestra plays in 1990-91, up from about 5% in the seasons around it. It is the largest anniversary bump in the data.

events.title: After September 11
events.text: Lorin Maazel conducts the world premiere of John Adams’s On the Transmigration of Souls, a Philharmonic commission for the first anniversary of the attacks.

sources.text: Wikipedia: On the Transmigration of Souls

events.title: Pyongyang
events.text: Maazel and the orchestra play in North Korea, at the East Pyongyang Grand Theatre.

events.title: The NY Phil Biennial
events.text: A new-music festival opens at MoMA. With the CONTACT! series (from 2009), it is one of the Alan Gilbert-era homes for living composers.

events.title: The shutdown
events.text: The last concert in Geffen Hall before COVID-19. The 2020-21 season is pop-ups: 46 NY Phil Bandwagon truck performances, 25 virtual concerts, small shows at The Shed and in parks.

events.title: A new Geffen Hall
events.text: The rebuilt hall reopens. From 2021-22 through 2025-26, living composers average 23% of performances, a level last reached in the five seasons to 1963-64.
